newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's president to wait for Congress vote to act.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's president to wait for Congress vote to act.

text.p: Ecuador's interim president appeared ready on Monday to oppose a plan that would hand over power to the head of Congress as a key adviser said she had never agreed to such a deal.

Rosalia Arteaga, the first woman president in Ecuador's 167-year history, was appointed head of a caretaker governmnent on Sunday as part of an apparent agreement between lawmakers and the armed forces.

The deal aimed at ending a political crisis that erupted on Thursday when flamboyant populist Abdala Bucaram, known as "El Loco" (the madman), was ousted by a divided Congress on grounds of "mental incompetence" after two days of paralysing strikes over government austerity measures.

Congressional sources said the deal included an understanding that Arteaga, a 40-year-old lawyer and former education minister, would step down within a few days once Congress voted its leader Fabian Alarcon in to run the country until new elections could be held.
But Gil Barragan, whom Arteaga appointed as her interior minister on Sunday, said, "Rosalia never made any deal."
"Rosalia will make a decision after Congress votes," Fausto Jaramillo, another adviser, said.
"If Congress elects a president without reforming the Constitution, we could declare the vote unconstitutional and go home or we could stay here until they kill us," he added.

"I'm afraid we're on the verge of a new conflict," Quito Mayor Jamil Mahuad said of the standoff. He said he was a participant in talks at the Defence Ministry where the "transition deal" was hammered out before dawn Sunday.
"Arteaga gave her word that she would only stay in power until Tuesday," the mayor said.

Alarcon, the only visible candidate to take power from Arteaga, could have a difficult time mustering the necessary votes to pass a constitutional reform. This is especially true if Bucaram -- who was rumoured to be planning to hand over to Arteaga after his ouster by a 44-34 vote -- works as expected to block Alarcon's power grab.
Earlier, the United States had praised the willingness of Ecuador's political leaders to resolve the country's crisis peacefully and praised the military's role as honourable.

"We were heartened by the fact that the military and the national police had essentially allowed the politicians to work out what appears to be a political compromise ... an agreement in principle that would retain politcal stability," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
Alarcon had been voted in as president on Thursday but Bucaram refused to step down until Sunday when the defence minister quit and the plan to hand over interim power to Arteaga was announced.

Angered by Arteaga's comments at her news conference, where she vowed to remain in office "as long as necessary to restore democratic order," Alarcon said the accord paving the way for him to take over as president specified that he could be appointed by a simple majority of Congress, without any constitutional reforms.

An extraordinary session of Congress at which Alarcon has said he will be duly appointed president is set for 4 p.m. (2100 GMT) on Tuesday. "No (constitutional) reforms will be dealt with on Tuesday, no reforms are needed," he said.

The military, which has proved itself to be the ultimate power-broker in Ecuador, has yet to comment on the battle between Arteaga and Alarcon. But armed forces chief Gen. Paco Moncayo, who Arteaga aides say has been offered the defence ministry, was in closed-door talks with her at the ornate Carondelet presidential palace on Monday, palace sources said.
